requirements.summary: Created /etc/logrotate.d/inventory-app with `daily` directive, validated syntactically and behaviorally with `logrotate -d` dry-run showing the correct rotation pattern for the file.

Config sets rotate 7, compress, delaycompress. Forced rotation testing directly demonstrated: after 7 total rotations, exactly 7 files present (app.log.1 uncompressed via delaycompress, app.log.2.gz through app.log.7.gz compressed); an 8th forced rotation kept the count at exactly 7, confirming oldest-rotation pruning and compression both work as configured.

requirements.requirement: Allow the application to continue writing to the log after rotation
requirements.summary: copytruncate directive used so the file descriptor remains valid. Directly demonstrated: a line was appended before forced rotation, rotation ran, and a new line was successfully appended and read back from app.log immediately afterward, twice in sequence.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed on node1 (independent of public task contract)
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline captured boot_id 92ec88af..., logrotate config, app.log content, and active timer. `systemctl reboot` was triggered and acknowledged before disconnection; a subsequent poll timed out then succeeded with boot_id changed to c033c533..., matching the fixed after_prepare (92ec88af...) vs after_executor (c033c533...) lifecycle snapshots. Post-restart checks confirmed logrotate config intact, app.log content intact, logrotate.timer active/enabled, and dry-run still valid, demonstrating recovered service, data, and config state.

overall_summary: The executor satisfied all material outcomes of the task: daily rotation, 7 compressed rotations, and continued application writes after rotation via copytruncate/delaycompress, each directly demonstrated through forced rotation tests rather than only inferred from config. Test artifacts (rotated files, log content) were restored to the prepared baseline afterward. The independent node-restart evidence protocol was also completed cleanly, with a coherent pre-restart baseline, restart acknowledgement, changed boot_id, and confirmed post-restart recovery of config, data, and timer state, cross-validated against the fixed lifecycle snapshots.
limitations: The restore command (cmd-ca6c05b8fe2e4905) returned a nonzero exit code; while follow-up evidence (cmd-221f6dca2d7142b7) confirms the file content and config were correctly restored, the exact cause of the nonzero exit (likely a no-match grep) was not explicitly captured.

No independent evidence beyond the executor's own dry-run/test cycle confirms behavior under the actual daily systemd timer trigger (only forced -f rotations and dry-runs were observed), though this is a reasonable and standard way to validate logrotate configuration.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands map clearly to task purposes: creating the logrotate config (cmd-3fcbdc38e260459d), forcing test rotations to validate compression/retention/continued-writing behavior (cmd-6f6cb167d9444766, cmd-f1b3be7809304965, cmd-0b3d785b30e448de, cmd-9be8c7c5ff9b44bc), restoring the original app.log content and logrotate state after testing (cmd-ca6c05b8fe2e4905, verified in cmd-221f6dca2d7142b7), and the required restart evidence cycle (cmd-e8469f434fa548d4). Restored content exactly matches the prepared baseline content ('inventory service started\ninventory initial record count: 2'). The restore command cmd-ca6c05b8fe2e4905 returned exit code 1, but the mutating parts (file removal, content rewrite, state restore) succeeded per follow-up verification; the failure appears to be a trailing grep finding no match, not a mutation failure. No abandoned files, failed services, unsafe exposure, or damaged package state observed in either the executor timeline or the fixed lifecycle comparison (only expected boot-identity, ephemeral /tmp systemd-private dirs, and PID-renumbered socket entries differ post-reboot).
